chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah ibn Ayyub from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said:

"The one who performs i'tikaf in Mecca may pray in whichever of its houses he wishes; it is the same for him whether he prays in the mosque or in its houses." This is not contradictory to what we have previously stated, that there is no i'tikaf except in the specific mosques, because what this report entails is the permissibility of prayer outside the mosque, without i'tikaf, and this is not prevented from it, because in the case of necessity, if a person leaves the mosque in Mecca and the time for prayer enters, it is permissible for him to pray in whichever place he wishes. And the ruling for other mosques is not like this: not that it is not permissible for him to pray until he returns to the mosque in which he performed i'tikaf. And that which clarifies what we mentioned is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: Can a person performing i'tikaf in Mecca pray in houses other than the mosque?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the juristic distinction between the general requirement of i'tikaf in designated mosques and the unique flexibility granted to those in Mecca, where prayer locations are not restricted to the mosque itself. Scholars explain that this does not negate the core definition of i'tikaf but rather reflects the permissibility of praying anywhere in Mecca due to its sanctity, distinguishing it from other mosques where one must remain within the specific premises. This ruling underscores the special status of Mecca in Shia fiqh, where the boundaries of ritual space are more expansive compared to other sacred sites.
